sentences.l: Then the spirit began to spew with embers, to burn bright dwellings, — the burning-light stood to men in hostility;
sentences.n: ‘Ðā se gæst’ is ‘then the spirit’, the dragon (‘gæst’ ‘spirit, creature’). ‘glēdum’ is a dative of means, ‘with embers’, after ‘spīwan’ ‘to spew’; ‘beorht hofu’ ‘bright dwellings’ is the object of ‘bærnan’ ‘to burn’. After the dash, ‘brynelēoma’ is ‘burning-light’ (‘bryne’ ‘burning’ + ‘lēoma’ ‘light, gleam’), the glare of the flames. It is the subject of ‘stōd’, and ‘eldum on andan’ means ‘to men in hostility’ (‘eldum’ dative plural of ‘ylde’ ‘men’; ‘andan’ dative of ‘anda’ ‘malice, enmity’); I take the whole to mean the fire was a horror to them, a loose rendering of an idiom. Last night’s raid is the dragon’s answer to the stolen cup.
sentences.i: Then the creature began to spit out embers and to burn the bright dwellings; the glare of the fire was a terror to men;

sentences.t:
nō ðǣr āht cwices
lāð lyftfloga lǣfan wolde.
sentences.l: not there anything of the living would the hateful air-flier leave.
sentences.n: ‘āht cwices’ is ‘anything of a living thing’, ‘cwices’ a partitive genitive depending on ‘āht’, the object of ‘lǣfan’ ‘to leave (alive)’; ‘nō … wolde’ is ‘would not’. ‘lāð’ is ‘hateful’ and ‘lyftfloga’ ‘air-flier’ (‘lyft’ ‘air’ + ‘floga’ ‘flier’, from ‘flēogan’ ‘fly’), the dragon again; the same ‘-floga’ turns up in ‘wīdflogan’ at 2346.
sentences.i: the hateful flier through the air meant to leave nothing living there.

sentences.t:
Wæs þæs wyrmes wīg wīde gesȳne,
nearofāges nīð nēan ond feorran,
hū se gūðsceaða Gēata lēode
hatode ond hȳnde;
sentences.l: Was the worm’s war widely seen, the narrow-foe’s malice near and far, how the war-scather hated and afflicted the Geats’ people;
sentences.n: ‘wyrmes’ is ‘the worm’s’ (the house rendering of ‘wyrm’), a genitive with ‘wīg’, here ‘attack, war’, and ‘gesȳne’ is ‘visible’ (the adjective ‘gesīene’). ‘nearofāges’ is a genitive too, ‘of the narrow-foe’ (‘nearo’ ‘narrow, cruel’ + ‘fāh’ ‘hostile’; I think found only here, and the sense ‘cruel-hostile’ is a guess), with ‘nīð’ ‘malice’. ‘hū’ opens a clause saying what was seen: ‘se gūðsceaða’, ‘the war-scather’ (‘sceaða’ ‘one who harms’, as in ‘ūhtsceaða’ ‘dawn-scather’), ‘hatode ond hȳnde’, ‘hated and afflicted’ (‘hȳnan’ ‘humble, injure’), with ‘Gēata lēode’ ‘Geats’ people’ as object.
sentences.i: The dragon’s onslaught was seen far and wide, the cruel enemy’s spite near and far, how the war-scather hated the people of the Geats and brought them low;

sentences.t:
hord eft gescēat,
dryhtsele dyrnne ǣr dæges hwīle.
sentences.l: the hoard again he sped to, the lord-hall secret, before the day’s while.
sentences.n: ‘hord eft gescēat’ is ‘he sped again to the hoard’; ‘gescēotan’ (‘shoot, rush’) with the hoard as goal is a guess at the construction. ‘dryhtsele dyrnne’ is ‘the secret lord-hall’ (‘dryht’ ‘troop, lord’ + ‘sele’ ‘hall’), in apposition to ‘hord’; the barrow is grimly called a lord’s hall. ‘ǣr dæges hwīle’ is ‘before the day’s while’, which I read as before daybreak.
sentences.i: It sped back to its hoard, its secret hall, before the coming of day.

sentences.t:
Hæfde landwara līge befangen,
bǣle ond bronde;
sentences.l: The land-warden had enclosed (them) with fire, with blaze and brand;
sentences.n: The subject is ‘landwara’, a nominative singular (‘land’ + ‘-wara’, ‘warden, dweller’), the dragon; ‘land-defender’ and ‘land-dweller’ are both possible, so the sense is partly a guess. ‘Hæfde … befangen’ makes a pluperfect, ‘had enclosed’ (‘befōn’ ‘surround, seize’), and the object is not stated: the Geats and their dwellings, from the lines before. ‘līge’, ‘bǣle ond bronde’ are datives of means (‘līg’ ‘flame’, ‘bǣl’ ‘blaze, pyre’, ‘brond’ ‘brand’), stacked three deep for emphasis.
sentences.i: The warden of the land had wrapped them in flame, in blaze and burning brand;

sentences.t:
beorges getrūwọde,
wīges ond wealles; him sēo wēn gelēah.
sentences.l: in the barrow he trusted, in war and in the wall; to him the hope lied.
sentences.n: ‘getrūwọde’ is ‘trusted’, and ‘trūwian’ here takes the genitive (it takes the dative too, as at 2370): ‘beorges’ ‘of the barrow’, ‘wīges ond wealles’ ‘of war and of the wall’. This is the first vowel in this part with a dot beneath (ọ), which is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. ‘him sēo wēn gelēah’ is ‘to him the hope lied’: ‘gelēogan’ ‘deceive’ takes the dative, and ‘wēn’ is ‘expectation, hope’. The barrow’s wall is the stone that protected the hoard, and he finds it no protection against a king’s vengeance.
sentences.i: he trusted in his barrow, in his fighting and his wall; but his hope betrayed him.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs Bīowulfe brōga gecȳðed
snūde tō sōðe, þæt his sylfes hām,
bolda sēlest brynewylmum mealt,
gifstōl Gēata.
sentences.l: Then was to Beowulf the terror made known quickly for truth, that his own home, the best of halls, in burning-surges melted, the gift-seat of the Geats.
sentences.n: ‘brōga’ is ‘terror’, the subject of ‘wæs gecȳðed’, ‘was made known’, to ‘Bīowulfe’ (dative), ‘snūde tō sōðe’ ‘quickly, for a truth’. The ‘þæt’-clause says what the terror was: ‘his sylfes hām’, ‘his own home’, ‘bolda sēlest’, ‘best of halls’ (genitive plural, partitive), and ‘gifstōl Gēata’, ‘the gift-seat of the Geats’ (as at 168), all in apposition, with ‘mealt’, ‘melted’ (‘meltan’ ‘be consumed’), and ‘brynewylmum’, ‘with burning-surges’ (‘bryne’ ‘burning’ + ‘wylm’ ‘surge, welling’). ‘hām’ has Klaeber’s italic ‘ā’: the manuscript has ‘him’, and Grundtvig read ‘hām’.
sentences.i: Then the dreadful news was swiftly made known to Beowulf as the truth: that his own home, the best of halls, the gift-throne of the Geats, had melted in surging flames.

sentences.t:
Þæt ðām gōdan wæs
hrēow on hreðre, hygesorga mǣst;
sentences.l: That to the good man was grief in the breast, the greatest of mind-sorrows;
sentences.n: ‘Þæt’ is the news just given, and ‘ðām gōdan’ is ‘to the good man’, a dative, Beowulf. ‘wæs hrēow’ is ‘was grief’, ‘hrēow’ here a noun ‘sorrow’ (a word that also means ‘rue, repentance’), ‘on hreðre’ ‘in the breast’. ‘hygesorga mǣst’ is ‘greatest of mind-sorrows’, a partitive genitive plural (‘hyge’ ‘mind’ + ‘sorg’ ‘sorrow’).
sentences.i: That was heart-grief to the good man, the greatest sorrow of his mind;

sentences.l: thought the wise one that he had bitterly angered the Wielder, the eternal Lord, against ancient right;
sentences.n: ‘wēnde’ is ‘thought, supposed’, ‘se wīsa’ ‘the wise one’ (here the adjective ‘wise’ used as a noun, not the noun ‘wīsa’ ‘leader’ of 259), and the ‘þæt’-clause is in the subjunctive: ‘gebulge’, ‘had angered’, from ‘gebelgan’. It takes datives, ‘Wealdende’ and ‘ēcean Dryhtne’ (‘Wielder’ and ‘eternal Lord’, as for God in the Prologue and at 1691). ‘ofer ealde riht’ is ‘beyond (against) ancient right’, ‘riht’ ‘law’; the poet does not say what Beowulf thinks he broke. ‘bitre’ is ‘bitterly’. The thought is only Beowulf’s fear.
sentences.i: the wise man thought that he had bitterly angered the Ruler, the eternal Lord, by breaking ancient law;

sentences.t:
brēost innan wēoll
þēostrum geþoncum, swā him geþȳwe ne wæs.
sentences.l: the breast within welled with dark thoughts, as to him was not usual.
sentences.n: ‘brēost innan wēoll’ is ‘the breast welled within’ (‘weallan’ ‘well up, seethe’, ‘wēoll’ its past), ‘þēostrum geþoncum’ ‘with dark thoughts’, a dative of means. ‘swā him geþȳwe ne wæs’ is ‘as was not usual to him’; I take ‘geþȳwe’ as ‘customary’ (from ‘þēaw’ ‘custom’), a rare word, so the sense is partly a guess.
sentences.i: his heart within him seethed with dark thoughts, as was not his way.

sentences.l: Had the fire-dragon the people’s stronghold, the island from without, that earth-ward, ground down with embers;
sentences.n: The subject is ‘līgdraca’ ‘fire-dragon’ (‘līg’ ‘flame’ + ‘draca’ ‘dragon’); ‘Hæfde … forgrunden’ is ‘had ground down, destroyed’ (‘forgrindan’), with ‘glēdum’ ‘with embers’. The objects, in apposition, are ‘lēoda fæsten’ ‘the people’s stronghold’ and ‘ēalond’ ‘island, water-land’ (‘ēa’ ‘water’ + ‘land’); ‘ūtan’ is the adverb ‘from without’, so ‘the island on its outer side’; which part of the land is meant, perhaps the coast, is a guess. ‘eorðweard ðone’ (‘ðone’ the accusative ‘that’) is the hard part. ‘eorðweard’ is not found elsewhere; I read ‘earth-ward’, a land-defence, which is a guess. Sweet suggested ‘eorðgeard’ (‘earth-yard’), and other editors alter ‘ðone’ to ‘ðonne’.
sentences.i: The fire-dragon had ruined with its embers the people’s stronghold, their island-land on its outer side, that fortress of the earth;

sentences.t:
him ðæs gūðkyning,
Wedera þīoden wræce leornode.
sentences.l: for him for that the war-king, the Weders’ famed lord, devised vengeance.
sentences.n: ‘him ðæs’ is ‘against him for that’, ‘him’ the dragon and ‘ðæs’ a genitive of cause. The subject is ‘gūðkyning’ ‘war-king’ (as at 199), in apposition with ‘Wedera þīoden’ ‘the Weders’ famed lord’. ‘wræce leornode’ is literally ‘learned vengeance’; ‘leornian’ ‘learn’ here means ‘find out, devise’, which I take as the sense, though the idiom is a guess.
sentences.i: For this the war-king, the lord of the Weders, planned vengeance on him.

sentences.l: Bade for himself then make the shelter of warriors, the lord of earls, an all-iron war-board, a wondrous one;
sentences.n: ‘Heht … gewyrcean’ is ‘bade (them) make’, with ‘him’ ‘for himself’; the subject is ‘wīgendra hlēo’ ‘shelter of warriors’ (as of Hrothgar at 429), in apposition with ‘eorla dryhten’ ‘lord of earls’. ‘wīgbord’ is ‘war-board’, a shield (‘bord’ ‘board, shield’), ‘wrǣtlīc’ ‘wondrous, curious’, and ‘eallīrenne’ is ‘all-iron’ (‘eall’ ‘all’ + ‘īren’ ‘iron’), an accusative with a masculine ending although ‘bord’ is neuter, so it does not agree with ‘wīgbord’ as it stands. That is why some editors add a missing masculine word, ‘scyld’ ‘shield’ (Bugge, Holthausen); Klaeber does not.
sentences.i: Then the protector of warriors, the lord of earls, ordered a wonderful war-shield to be made for him, all of iron;

sentences.t:
wisse hē gearwe,
þæt him holtwudu he(lpan) ne meahte,
lind wið līge.
sentences.l: he knew well that to him forest-wood could not (help), linden against flame.
sentences.n: ‘wisse hē gearwe’ is ‘he knew well’, the past of ‘witan’. ‘holtwudu’ is ‘forest-wood’ (‘holt’ ‘wood’ + ‘wudu’ ‘wood’, as at 1369), and ‘lind’ ‘linden’ is a shield of that wood, so the two stand in apposition. ‘he(lpan)’ has its last letters in parentheses because they are lost from the manuscript; Thorkelin’s transcript has them. ‘ne meahte’ is ‘could not’. ‘wið līge’ is ‘against fire’.
sentences.i: he knew well that a shield of wood could not help him against the flame.

sentences.t:
Sceolde lǣndaga
æþeling ǣrgōd ende gebīdan,
worulde līfes, ond se wyrm somod,
þēah ðe hordwelan hēolde lange.
sentences.l: Had to, of his lent days, the atheling good-from-of-old await the end, of life in the world, and the worm together, though he had held the hoard-wealth long.
sentences.n: ‘Sceolde’ is ‘had to, was fated to’, with ‘æþeling ǣrgōd’ as subject (‘atheling good-from-of-old’, as at 130) and ‘ende gebīdan’ ‘to await the end’. ‘lǣndaga’ has Klaeber’s italic ‘lǣn’: the manuscript has ‘þend’, and Kemble read ‘lǣn-’, ‘loan’, so ‘days on loan’, life as something lent. ‘worulde līfes’ is ‘of life in the world’ (genitives). ‘ond se wyrm somod’ is ‘and the dragon together (with him)’. ‘þēah ðe … hēolde’ is ‘though he had held’, the dragon, ‘hordwelan’ ‘hoard-wealth’.
sentences.i: The prince, good from of old, was to meet the end of his borrowed days, the end of his life in the world, and the dragon with him, though it had held the hoard-wealth long.

sentences.l: Scorned then the ring-prince that he the wide-flier with a troop should seek, with a broad host;
sentences.n: ‘Oferhogode’ is ‘scorned, thought it beneath him’ (‘oferhogian’), with a ‘þæt’-clause in the subjunctive, ‘gesōhte’ ‘should seek’. ‘hringa fengel’ is ‘ring-prince’ (‘fengel’ ‘prince’, as of Hrothgar at 1474), Beowulf. ‘wīdflogan’ is ‘wide-flier’ (‘wīd’ ‘wide’ + ‘floga’ ‘flier’), the dragon; the datives ‘weorode’ ‘with a troop’ and ‘sīdan herge’ ‘with a broad army’ say how he would have gone.
sentences.i: Then the prince of rings scorned to seek out the far-flier with a company, with a great army;

sentences.t:
nō hē him þā sæcce ondrēd,
nē him þæs wyrmes wīg for wiht dyde,
eafoð ond ellen, forðon hē ǣr fela
nearo nēðende nīða gedīgde,
hildehlemma, syððan hē Hrōðgāres,
sigorēadig secg, sele fǣlsode,
ond æt gūðe forgrāp Grendeles mǣgum
lāðan cynnes.
sentences.l: not he for himself that fight dreaded, nor for himself counted the worm’s war for a whit, its strength and courage, because he formerly many narrows, daring, of battles came through, of battle-crashes, since he, Hrothgar’s, the victory-blessed man, hall cleansed, and in battle crushed Grendel’s kinsmen of the hateful race.
sentences.n: ‘nō hē … ondrēd’ is ‘he did not dread’, the object ‘þā sæcce’ ‘that fight’. ‘þā’ has Klaeber’s italic ‘ā’: the manuscript has ‘hī þā’, which would be ‘him þām’ with ‘þām’ a dative; his ‘him þā’ (Kemble’s) makes ‘þā’ the accusative ‘that’ and ‘him’ a reflexive dative. ‘nē him … for wiht dyde’ is ‘nor did he count for a whit’, the object ‘þæs wyrmes wīg’ ‘the worm’s war’, with ‘eafoð ond ellen’ ‘strength and courage’ in apposition. ‘forðon’ opens the reason: ‘fela nearo’ ‘many narrows’ (‘nearo’ ‘strait, peril’, accusative plural), ‘nēðende’ ‘daring’ (participle of ‘nēþan’ ‘venture’), ‘nīða’ ‘of battles’ and ‘hildehlemma’ ‘of battle-crashes’, genitives, and ‘gedīgde’ ‘came through’. ‘syððan’ ‘since’ gives the point in time: the cleansing of ‘sele’ ‘hall’ by ‘sigorēadig secg’ ‘the victory-blessed man’. ‘forgrāp’ ‘crushed’ takes the dative ‘Grendeles mǣgum’; ‘lāðan cynnes’ ‘of the hateful race’ is a genitive (Trautmann and Holthausen write ‘cynne’).
sentences.i: He did not dread the fight, nor did he reckon the dragon’s warfare worth a whit, its strength and courage, since in earlier days, in his daring, he had come through many a tight corner, many a clash of battle, ever since, blessed with victory, he cleansed Hrothgar’s hall and crushed in battle the kinsmen of Grendel, that hateful race.

sentences.t:
Nō þæt lǣsest wæs
hondgemōt[a], þǣr mon Hygelāc slōh,
syððan Gēata cyning gūðe rǣsum,
frēawine folca Frēslondum on,
Hrēðles eafora hiorodryncum swealt,
bille gebēaten.
sentences.l: Not that the least was of hand-meetings, where Hygelac one struck down, after the Geats’ king in the rushes of war, the noble friend of peoples, in the Frisian lands, Hrethel’s heir, in the sword-drinks died, beaten by the blade.
sentences.n: ‘Nō þæt lǣsest wæs hondgemōt[a]’ is ‘that was not the least of hand-meetings’ (‘lǣsest’ ‘least’; ‘hondgemōta’ a genitive plural, ‘hand-meetings’, hand-to-hand fights). The manuscript has ‘gemot’ and Kemble supplied the bracketed ‘a’. ‘mon Hygelāc slōh’ is ‘one struck Hygelac’, ‘mon’ the indefinite ‘one’. In the ‘syððan’ clause the subject is ‘Gēata cyning’ ‘the Geats’ king’, in apposition with ‘frēawine folca’ ‘noble friend of peoples’ and ‘Hrēðles eafora’ ‘Hrethel’s heir’; the verb is ‘swealt’ ‘died’ (‘sweltan’), ‘Frēslondum on’ ‘in the Frisian lands’, ‘gūðe rǣsum’ ‘in the rushes of war’ (‘rǣs’ ‘rush’), ‘hiorodryncum’ ‘in sword-drinks’ (‘heoru’ ‘sword’ + ‘drync’ ‘drink’, the sword drinking blood), and ‘bille gebēaten’ ‘beaten with the blade’. This is Hygelac’s fatal raid on the Frisians, told earlier by Beowulf and the poet.
sentences.i: That was not the least of the hand-to-hand fights, in which Hygelac was struck down, when the king of the Geats, the noble friend of peoples, Hrethel’s son, died in the Frisian lands, in the rush of battle and the slaughter of swords, beaten down by the blade.

sentences.t:
Þonan Bīowulf cōm
sylfes cræfte, sundnytte drēah;
sentences.l: Thence Beowulf came by his own skill, swim-use he did;
sentences.n: ‘Þonan’ is ‘from there’, the Frisian land. ‘sylfes cræfte’ is ‘by his own skill’ (‘sylfes’ a genitive ‘of himself’; ‘cræft’ ‘skill, strength’, dative of means), and ‘sundnytte drēah’ ‘practised swim-use’ (‘sund’ ‘swimming’ + ‘nytt’ ‘use’; ‘drēogan’ ‘do, carry out’), with ‘sundnytte’ the object and swimming the skill meant by ‘cræfte’.
sentences.i: From there Beowulf came away by his own skill, making use of his swimming;

sentences.t:
hæfde him on earme (āna) þrītig
hildegeatwa, þā hē tō holme (st)āg.
sentences.l: he had on his arm alone thirty battle-gear, when he to the sea stepped.
sentences.n: ‘hæfde him on earme’ is ‘had on his arm’, ‘him’ a reflexive dative. ‘(āna)’ is Grein’s restoration of a lost word, ‘alone’; the apparatus gives the manuscript here as lost letters and then ‘xxx’, the numeral for ‘þrītig’ ‘thirty’. ‘hildegeatwa’ is ‘battle-gear’, accusative plural (‘geatwe’ ‘equipment’). ‘(st)āg’ is Kemble’s restoration of ‘stāg’ (‘stīgan’ ‘go, step’), and ‘tō holme’ means ‘to the sea’ (‘holm’ ‘sea, wave’).
sentences.i: he had on his arm, alone, thirty sets of battle-gear, when he went down into the sea.

sentences.l: Not at all had the Hetware cause to exult in foot-fighting, who in front against him bore shields of linden;
sentences.n: ‘Nealles’ is ‘not at all’; ‘Hetware’ are the Hetware (a Frankish people) and ‘hrēmge’ ‘exulting’ (‘hrēmig’) the adjective agreeing with them. ‘þorf(t)on’ is ‘had need, had cause’, the plural past of ‘þurfan’, with the ‘t’ Kemble’s restoration; ‘fēðewīges’ is a genitive, ‘of foot-war’ (‘fēþe’ ‘foot-troop’ + ‘wīg’), and the same ‘fēþe’ is in ‘fēþecempa’. ‘þē’ ‘who’ opens the relative clause, ‘foran ongēan’ ‘face to face’, ‘linde’ ‘linden-shields’ (accusative plural), ‘bǣron’ ‘bore’.
sentences.i: The Hetware had no cause to exult in their fighting on foot, those who carried their shields against him;

sentences.t:
lȳt eft becwōm
fram þām hildfrecan hāmes nīosan!
sentences.l: few came back from that battle-bold man to seek home!
sentences.n: ‘lȳt’ is ‘few’, the subject of ‘becwōm’ ‘came’, ‘eft’ ‘back’. ‘fram þām hildfrecan’ is ‘from that battle-bold one’ (‘hild’ ‘battle’ + ‘freca’ ‘bold one’), Beowulf, and ‘hāmes nīosan’ ‘to seek home’ (‘nīosan’ ‘visit, seek’, taking the genitive). The exclamation mark is Klaeber’s.
sentences.i: few of them came back from that fierce warrior to see their homes again!

sentences.t:
Oferswam ðā sioleða bigong sunu Ecgðēowes,
earm ānhaga eft tō lēodum;
sentences.l: Swam over then the son of Ecgtheow the seals’ range, a wretched lone-man, back to his people;
sentences.n: ‘Oferswam’ is ‘swam across’, the subject ‘sunu Ecgðēowes’ ‘Ecgtheow’s son’. ‘sioleða bigong’ is ‘the seals’ range’, the sea, and is a guess: ‘sioleða’ is a form I cannot parallel, which I take as a genitive plural ‘of seals’; one editor (Thorpe) wrote ‘siol-ēðel’ (‘seal-homeland’), Bouterwek ‘seolhbaða’ (‘seals’ baths’), and Grein ‘siolēða’ (‘sea-waves’). ‘earm ānhaga’ is ‘wretched solitary one’, ‘ānhaga’ (‘ān’ ‘one’ + ‘haga’, perhaps ‘enclosure’, a guess at the second part) meaning one who goes alone. ‘eft tō lēodum’ is ‘back to the people’.
sentences.i: Then the son of Ecgtheow swam back across the seals’ range to his own people, a pitiable man alone;

sentences.t:
þǣr him Hygd gebēad hord ond rīce,
bēagas ond bregostōl;
sentences.l: where to him Hygd offered the hoard and the realm, rings and the princely seat;
sentences.n: ‘þǣr’ is ‘where’, ‘him’ the dative ‘to him’, Beowulf, and ‘gebēad’ the past of ‘gebēodan’ ‘offer’. Hygd is Hygelac’s queen. The objects are ‘hord ond rīce’ ‘hoard and realm’ and ‘bēagas ond bregostōl’ ‘rings and princely seat’ (‘brego’ ‘prince’ + ‘stōl’ ‘seat’, as at 2194).
sentences.i: There Hygd offered him the hoard and the kingdom, the rings and the royal throne;

sentences.t:
bearne ne trūwọde,
þæt hē wið ælfylcum ēþelstōlas
healdan cūðe, ðā wæs Hygelāc dēad.
sentences.l: in her child she did not trust, that he against foreign peoples the ancestral seats could hold, when Hygelac was dead.
sentences.n: ‘bearne ne trūwọde’ is ‘in the child she did not trust’; ‘trūwian’ takes the dative here, and the subject is Hygd (the dot under ‘ọ’ is Klaeber’s metrical sign again). The ‘bearn’ is her son Heardred, named at 2375. ‘þæt hē … cūðe’ is ‘that he could’ (‘cunnan’ ‘be able’), ‘healdan’ ‘to hold’, ‘ēþelstōlas’ ‘ancestral seats’ (‘ēþel’ ‘homeland’ + ‘stōl’). ‘wið ælfylcum’ is ‘against foreign peoples’ (‘el-’ ‘other’ + ‘folc’, a dative plural), and ‘ðā wæs Hygelāc dēad’ ‘when Hygelac was dead’.
sentences.i: but she did not trust her son to be able to hold the ancestral seats against foreign peoples, now that Hygelac was dead.

sentences.t:
Nō ðȳ ǣr fēasceafte findan meahton
æt ðām æðelinge ǣnige ðinga,
þæt hē Heardrēde hlāford wǣre,
oððe þone cynedōm cīosan wolde;
sentences.l: Not the sooner could the destitute find from the atheling in any way that he to Heardred lord would be, or would choose that kingship;
sentences.n: ‘Nō ðȳ ǣr’ is ‘none the sooner’, ‘ðȳ’ an instrumental. The subject is ‘fēasceafte’, ‘the destitute’ (‘fēasceaft’ as at 2283 and in the Prologue), here the Geats left without a king; ‘meahton’ ‘could’, ‘findan æt ðām æðelinge’ ‘find from the atheling’, ‘ǣnige ðinga’ ‘in any way’; ‘ðām æðelinge’ is Beowulf. The one ‘þæt’-clause, with two verbs, says what they could not win: that he ‘Heardrēde hlāford wǣre’ (‘be lord to Heardred’, that is, Heardred’s lord, a dative) or ‘þone cynedōm cīosan wolde’ ‘would choose the kingship’ for himself.
sentences.i: The bereft Geats could not, for all that, win from the prince, in any way, that he would be Heardred’s lord, or that he would choose the kingship;

sentences.t:
hwæðre hē hine on folce frēondlārum hēold,
ēstum mid āre, oð ðæt hē yldra wearð,
Weder-Gēatum wēold.
sentences.l: yet he him among the people with friendly counsels upheld, with kindnesses and with honour, until he older became, ruled the Weder-Geats.
sentences.n: ‘hwæðre’ is ‘yet’, ‘hē’ Beowulf, ‘hine’ Heardred, the italic ‘ne’ being Klaeber’s alteration of the manuscript’s ‘hī’ (Thorpe wrote ‘hine’). ‘hēold’ is ‘supported, kept up’; ‘frēondlārum’ is ‘with friendly counsels’ (‘frēond’ ‘friend’ + ‘lār’ ‘teaching, counsel’), ‘ēstum’ ‘with kindnesses’, ‘mid āre’ ‘with honour’. ‘oð ðæt hē yldra wearð’ is ‘until he became older’ (a comparative). ‘wēold’ has no stated subject; I take Heardred, ruling the ‘Weder-Gēatum’ (dative), once of age, but that is a reading, since Beowulf as regent is also possible.
sentences.i: Yet he supported him among the people with friendly counsel, with kindness and honour, until he grew older and ruled the Geats.

sentences.t:
Hyne wræcmæcgas
ofer sǣ sōhtan, suna Ōhteres;
sentences.l: Him exiles over the sea sought, the sons of Ohthere;
sentences.n: ‘Hyne’ is ‘him’, Heardred, the object of ‘sōhtan’ ‘sought’, and the subject is ‘wræcmæcgas’ ‘exiles’ (‘wræc’ ‘exile’ + ‘mæcg’ ‘man’), named by ‘suna Ōhteres’ ‘the sons of Ohthere’. ‘ofer sǣ’ is ‘over the sea’; the exiles are Swedish princes who have fallen out with their own king.
sentences.i: Exiles came across the sea to find him, the sons of Ohthere;

sentences.t:
hæfdon hȳ forhealden helm Scylfinga,
þone sēlestan sǣcyninga
þāra ðe in Swīorīce sinc brytnade,
mǣrne þēoden.
sentences.l: they had held-amiss the helm of the Scylfings, the best of sea-kings of those who in Sweden treasure distributed, the famed prince.
sentences.n: ‘hæfdon hȳ forhealden’ is ‘they had … held amiss’: ‘forhealden’ is the participle of ‘forhealdan’ (‘for-’ ‘wrongly’ + ‘healdan’ ‘hold’), and I take it to mean they had rebelled against, withheld their loyalty from, the king, which is a guess at a rare verb. ‘helm Scylfinga’ is ‘helm of the Scylfings’ (‘helm’ ‘protector’), and ‘þone sēlestan sǣcyninga’ ‘the best of sea-kings’ (a partitive genitive) and ‘mǣrne þēoden’ ‘the famed prince’ are in apposition. ‘þāra ðe in Swīorīce sinc brytnade’ is ‘of those who in Sweden dispensed treasure’ (‘Swīorīce’ ‘Sweden’; ‘brytnian’ ‘distribute’). The king is not named here. The manuscript has ‘ðe’ twice and Kemble deletes one.
sentences.i: they had broken faith with the protector of the Scylfings, the best of the sea-kings who gave out treasure in Sweden, a famed lord.

sentences.t: Him þæt tō mearce wearð;
sentences.l: To him that for a boundary became;
sentences.n: ‘Him’ is Heardred and ‘þæt’ the harbouring of the exiles. ‘tō mearce wearð’ is ‘became to a boundary’ (‘mearc’ ‘mark, limit’), the limit of his life; the idiom is a guess. The unit starts mid-line after the period.
sentences.i: That became his end;

sentences.t:
hē þǣr [f]or feorme feorhwunde hlēat,
sweordes swengum, sunu Hygelāces;
sentences.l: he there for the entertainment a life-wound received, by the strokes of the sword, Hygelac’s son;
sentences.n: ‘hlēat’ is ‘received’ (‘hlēotan’ ‘obtain by lot’), the object ‘feorhwunde’ ‘life-wound’, a mortal one. ‘sweordes swengum’ is ‘by sword-strokes’ (a dative plural), and ‘sunu Hygelāces’ ‘son of Hygelac’ is Heardred. ‘[f]or feorme’ is Klaeber’s bracket and the sense is ‘for hospitality’ (‘feorm’ ‘food, entertainment’). The manuscript has ‘orfeorme’, as one word, which Klaeber divides and alters; Grein offered ‘on feorme’, ‘at the feast’, and four other editors print Klaeber’s reading. Taking it as ‘because of the hospitality he had given’ is my guess.
sentences.i: he got a mortal wound there for his hospitality, from the strokes of a sword, the son of Hygelac;

sentences.t:
ond him eft gewāt Ongẹnðīoes bearn
hāmes nīosan, syððan Heardrēd læg,
lēt ðone bregostōl Bīowulf healdan,
Gēatum wealdan;
sentences.l: and Ongentheow’s son went back again to seek home, after Heardred lay (dead), let Beowulf hold the princely seat, rule the Geats;
sentences.n: ‘Ongenðīoes bearn’ is the Swedish king, who turns home again (‘hāmes nīosan’ ‘to seek home’); the dot under ‘ẹ’ in ‘Ongẹnðīoes’ is again the metrical sign. ‘syððan Heardrēd læg’ is ‘after Heardred lay (dead)’. The subject of ‘lēt’ (‘let’) is still the king, and the infinitives ‘healdan’ ‘hold’ and ‘wealdan’ ‘rule’ (taking the dative ‘Gēatum’) are what he allowed; ‘bregostōl’ is ‘the princely seat’, as at 2370.
sentences.i: and Ongentheow’s son went home again, after Heardred lay dead, and let Beowulf hold the royal throne and rule the Geats;

sentences.t: þæt wæs gōd cyning.
sentences.l: that was a good king.
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is a neuter pronoun for a masculine person, an idiom of praise; the same words, ‘þæt wæs gōd cyning’, close the praise of Scyld in the Prologue. The words follow the naming of Beowulf as the man allowed to hold the throne, and I take them to praise him; the grammar alone would also fit the Swedish king who allowed it.
sentences.i: He was a good king.
